text: Only two people shared her special seat. <break time="0.8s" /> A fine old man in a velvet coat. <break time="0.8s" /> And a big old woman. <break time="0.8s" /> With a roll of knitting on her apron. <break time="0.8s" /> They did not speak. <break time="0.8s" /> Which was rather disappointing. <break time="0.8s" /> For Miss Brill always looked forward. <break time="0.8s" /> To the conversation every Sunday. <break time="0.8s" /> She had become quite expert. <break time="0.8s" /> She thought. <break time="0.8s" /> At listening as though she did not listen. <break time="0.8s" /> At sitting in other peoples lives. <break time="0.8s" /> Just for a minute. <break time="0.8s" /> While they talked around her. <break time="0.8s" /> Last Sunday. <break time="0.8s" /> An Englishman in a dreadful Panama hat. <break time="0.8s" /> And his wife in button boots. <break time="0.8s" /> Had sat there. <break time="0.8s" /> And the wife had talked the whole time. <break time="0.8s" /> About spectacles. <break time="0.8s" /> She knew she needed them. <break time="0.8s" /> But nothing her patient husband suggested. <break time="0.8s" /> Could please her. <break time="0.8s" /> And Miss Brill had wanted to shake her. <break time="0.8s" /> Now she watched the crowd. <break time="0.8s" /> The couples and groups. <break time="0.8s" /> Who were strolling to and fro. <break time="0.8s" /> Stopping to talk, to greet. <break time="0.8s" /> And to buy flowers from an old beggar. <break time="0.8s" /> Little children ran among them. <break time="0.8s" /> Swooping and laughing. <break time="0.8s" /> And when one small child. <break time="0.8s" /> Suddenly fell down. <break time="0.8s" /> Its mother rushed to the rescue. <break time="0.8s" /> Like a young hen. <break time="0.8s" /> Other people sat on the benches. <break time="0.8s" /> But they were odd, silent. <break time="0.8s" /> And nearly all old. <break time="0.8s" /> As if they had just come. <break time="0.8s" /> From dark little rooms. <break time="0.8s" /> Or even cupboards.
